newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Violence lingers as Guatemalans sign truce.
newsitem.headline: Violence lingers as Guatemalans sign truce.

text.p: Guatemala's government and leftist guerrillas signed a ceasefire in Oslo on Wednesday formally ending 36 years of fighting, but much work remains to eradicate endemic violence and human rights abuses in the Central American nation.

The scars of army butchery, which reached its height in the early 1980s with huge scorched-earth campaigns in rebel areas, will also take decades to heal. And a full accounting of the violence may never be completed.

"We can't say that with the ceasefire all of the human rights violations will stop. But these are steps being taken and one era is ending and we're entering another of work and implementation," said Lucia Quila, a leader of Conavigua, a widows' group formed in the 1980s.

President Alvaro Arzu has said repeatedly there have been no war-related casualties since early this year, when an informal ceasefire was put in place. That is cause for celebration given the extent of the killing during the military dictatorships of Gen. Romeo Lucas Garcia and Gen. Efrain Rios Montt from 1978-83.
"If it is necessary to turn the country into a cemetery in order to pacify it, I will not hesitate to do so," one of their strongman predecessors, President Carlos Arana, said in 1971.

In the past four years a series of exhumations of mass graves by international forensic specialists has only scratched the surface of the war violence. The conflict left more than 100,000 dead, mostly civilians, as well as an estimated 40,000 "disappeared" -- a euphemism for kidnapping and usually death at the hands of security forces.

The most numerous victims of the war were tens of thousands of Indian peasants killed in a series of massacres in the early 1980s as the government waged a campaign to eradicate guerrilla support in Guatemala's rural areas.

In 1978, the army massacred 100 Kekchi Indians at Panzos in eastern Guatemala. More than 2,500 Achi Indians were massacred during 1982 and 1983 in villages in the area around Rabinal, 50 miles (80 km) north of Guatemala City, including 268 men, women and children in the village of Plan de Sanchez.

The villages of Agua Fria and Las Dos RR in northern Guatemala were wiped off the map in the early 1980s and more than 750 people died in the two massacres. During a three-day orgy of violence in March 1982, 325 villagers in Cuarto Pueblo were killed, many burned alive. According to human rights observers, more than 2,500 villagers from Santiago Atitlan died or disappeared during the early 1980s.

Beginning in the late 1980s civilian governments began to wind down the war. But the army has remained the most powerful institution in the country and the last seven years have seen a string of notorious assassinations -- most of them unsolved and unpunished.

Eleven University of San Carlos students were assassinated in 1989 and sociologist Myrna Mack was stabbed to death on a street in the capital in September 1990. Politician and newspaper publisher Jorge Carpio and a Supreme Court judge were also killed in the 1990s.
A weak judicial system has been incapable of punishing officials accused of abuses.

Arzu has moved to cut back the army, agreeing as part of the peace accords to slash its ranks by one third next year. He also took the bold step of firing several corrupt members of the military top brass this year.
A final peace agreement will be signed on Dec. 29 in Guatemala City.
